tweets.text:
Any form of security through obscurity is fully over. This barely worked as a method with humans, but just simply is over in a world of autonomous systems that will look through every crevice and try every permutation of attack possible.

As a result, years and years of legacy enterprise infrastructure will need to be upgraded, security practices modernized, data pipelines cleaned up, access controls better managed, and much more. Agents will help on the defensive side because they can both accelerate this work and equally simulate the risk vectors.

But there’s a long road ahead to prepare for this future. This is also partially why diffusion timelines will take longer than some realize.

podcasts.name: Training Data
podcasts.title: David Silver and Lasse Espeholt of Ineffable Intelligence: A Superlearner for the Age of Experience
podcasts.transcript:
Speaker 1 | 00:00 - 00:32
Collectively, you know, we started with this kind of gray mush in our head. We somehow started out knowing nothing at all and somehow discovered, like, everything that humans know today was, like, this process of collective discovery, like, of of languages and technology and science and mathematics and all the rest of it. Know, everything we learned, we discovered it for ourselves. And that's an incredible thing that no one has cracked yet in AI. And so to me, that is the essence of what it will take to get to superintelligence, like a system that can just keep learning and discovering knowledge forever.

Speaker 2 | 00:49 - 01:10
I'm thrilled to have Dave Silver and Lesae Espeholt with us, two of the co founders of ineffable intelligence. Great name, by the way. Fun fact, Dave, you were the first person I cold emailed to come on training data when we started the show 100 ish episodes ago. And it feels like a full circle moment to finally have you on the show. So thank you for joining us.

Speaker 1 | 01:11 - 01:11
Thank you.

Speaker 2 | 01:12 - 01:43
Dave, let's start with you. Your 2009 PhD was on reinforcement learning applied to the devilishly difficult game of Go. You demonstrated for the world for the first time that superhuman in one domain machine intelligence was possible. And I think you were really the figure that inspired the entire current generation of reinforcement learning and deep learning researchers. And so thank you for your contributions to where the field is.

Speaker 2 | 01:44 - 01:57
I'm curious, thinking back to that point in time, what did you learn? What did you have conviction on? And what has remained the same and what has changed as AI has changed over the last five years or so?

Speaker 1 | 01:57 - 02:47
Yeah. Thank you, and pleasure to be here, and I'm glad I finally made it after these 100 episodes. It's a pleasure to be here. So I suppose I always had this conviction starting my PhD and going into the game of Go that the right approach to solve AI was through learning from experience, through systems that discovered things for themselves, that were learning through reinforcement learning to get better and better and better, and that that would be the thing which would lead to the emergence of intelligence and ultimately superintelligence. And so I suppose we were able to show that in the game of Go, but it's a conviction that has held true throughout my career, and here we are now applying that conviction, ineffable, trying to show that indeed superintelligence can emerge all the way through systems that learn from experience.

Speaker 1 | 02:48 - 03:39
And in terms of things which are different, although we are not pursuing the human data path that the LLM world has pursued, I do think there's lots of interesting lessons to learn from that. In particular, it was definitely a surprise to me how a system that was trained on a massive amount of data could then be very quickly fine tuned on a very small amount of data to completely change its behavior. That was something which I think was something which changed my mindset in terms of just suggesting that if you get things at the right scale, that a lot of things which seem incredibly hard or they might be very slow, that once you've kind of experienced enough data, that after that, the things that were slow can become very fast. I think that's a lesson that wasn't obvious to me in advance until it happened.

Speaker 2 | 03:39 - 03:56
Okay, we're going to come back to that later. You could have run this program inside DeepMind where could have probably had more access to compute than just about anybody. You decided the right thing to do was to start a new lab. Why'd you do that?

Speaker 1 | 03:57 - 04:31
Yeah. So look, first of all, I had a fantastic time at DeepMind. I loved my years there, and I have a huge amount of respect for the people there and still got on with them very well. But at the end of the day, I have a really strong belief about how we can go beyond where we are today with AI and all the way to superintelligence, And the path that I believe in doesn't actually go through LLM based products as an intermediate point. And when I really thought about that, I thought about it really hard.

Speaker 1 | 04:31 - 05:44
I realized that I felt that so passionately that this deserved to be more than just the corner of an organization that's focused on LLM based products and deserved to be represented by an elite AI lab that really just gives this approach its all and represents it 100%. Once I realized that, it felt very natural to create this company. I suppose another way to look at it is that the world already has tens of thousands, if not hundreds of thousands, of really talented researchers all pursuing exactly the same approach, really just doubling down on LLMs with pre training, post training, coding, and that kind of LLM path, am I going to be the 100,001 person that's pursuing that approach? Is that the most effective use of my time and my energy? And in the end, I realized that there's this other lamppost that right now no one is looking under and where if I actually put my effort there, has a much higher chance of really having a massive impact on the field because if this works, it's going to change the whole of AI.

Speaker 1 | 05:45 - 05:54
So I think that kind of realization also meant that this was something which just means that it's the best way to have impact upon the field through this approach.

Speaker 2 | 05:55 - 05:58
Plus, you had a company name that couldn't go to waste, so...

Speaker 1 | 05:58 - 05:58
That's right. Yeah, it's right.

Speaker 2 | 05:58 - 06:00
Do want to say where the mind's called Ineffable?

Speaker 1 | 06:00 - 06:54
Yeah. So I suppose the name ineffable, it came from this idea that there's really just knowledge could be so incredible, like the things which superintelligence will one day discover. This knowledge is going to be so unbelievable, incredible, and it's going to be something which is profoundly amazing and perhaps so profound that we can't even express it in human language. And so really, it's in line with this other path that doesn't go through human language based approaches, but instead build systems that discover things for themselves and has the possibility to discover knowledge that's unbelievably profound and ultimately ineffable. I should say there was also a secret second reason that we used, which was that this idea, it really has to work.

Speaker 1 | 06:54 - 07:07
Like, if you really just double down on learning from experience, it's an approach that just has to work. And so you could say that it can't possibly F up, so it's ineffable. So there you go. There's the secret reason as well with Amazing.

Speaker 2 | 07:07 - 07:20
Amazing. Best lab name. Leise, what about you? You were at Google. You were in a different group than Dave the deep learning group at DeepMind, and you spent years scaling up reinforcement learning on GPUs.

Speaker 2 | 07:20 - 07:26
What made you decide to leave DeepMind and what drew you to co found Ineffable?

Speaker 3 | 07:26 - 07:56
Right. So I joined DeepMind in January of 'fifteen and actually started working a bit with Dave around 'sixteen, I was doing this work on scaling up reinforcement learning. So as I said, I was part of the deep learning team and he was leading a reinforcement learning team, but we were working on an internal project together. I actually left DeepMind twice, so I left DeepMind in summer 'eighteen and went to Google Brain. Then eventually Google Brain and DeepMind merged, and then I was back again.

Speaker 3 | 07:57 - 08:18
But in the day, I left DeepMind again, like a year before Dave left. And the first time I heard about it, never was actually through one of our eventual investors. He was reaching out to me, asking what I thought about Dave. Well, my first reaction was, Dave, I missed out on an opportunity. I should have reached out to him.

Speaker 3 | 08:18 - 08:42
But I recall Dave as more often than not being one of the smartest people in the room. And shortly after that sync with that investor, they actually reached out to me. So I was like, great. Yeah, so I really love to work with Dave. I knew Wojciech and Chris from back in the day, and I thought the team was great.

Speaker 3 | 08:42 - 08:45
And I also thought it was amazing to have an opportunity like this in Europe.

Speaker 1 | 08:45 - 09:29
It should be said as well. We worked together on some of the early approaches to combining reinforcement learning with deep learning and trying to scale things up. And it should be said that Lasser, who, by the way, is very modest, he actually worked on some of the original approaches that were the first attempts to actually scale up reinforcement learning and show that it could be done at large scale and ways to paralyze reinforcement learning and ways to kind of build out architectures that were scalable. And if you look today at the way the field's gone, actually all of the ideas that people use today kind of of hail back to that original work that Lasser did back in the day. That's where all the roots come from of scaled up RL.

Speaker 1 | 09:29 - 09:31
So he was the first to figure it out.

Speaker 2 | 09:31 - 09:39
Wonderful. We should have you guys introduce each other instead of you. You're both too humble to brag about yourselves. Okay. Let's talk about ineffable and what you're building.

Speaker 2 | 09:40 - 09:53
You have a beautiful mission statement as a company. You're gonna build a super learner and make first contact with super intelligence. Can you define both of those things for us? What is a super learner and what does making first contact look like?

Speaker 1 | 09:53 - 10:23
Yeah. So to me, a super learner is something which is... It's got incredible capacity both in its depth of what it can learn and in its breadth. So in the depth dimension, it should be something that can start from not knowing anything at all and can go all the way through to discovering things that go way beyond what humans know. So an analogy to this would be the way that human collectively, we started with this kind of gray mush in our head.

Speaker 1 | 10:24 - 11:04
We somehow started out knowing nothing at all and somehow discovered everything that humans know today was this process of collective discovery, of languages and technology and science and mathematics and all the rest of it. Everything we learned, we discovered it for ourselves. It wasn't that someone came down and gave us a blueprint of how this should work, and it wasn't that someone came down and gave a trillion element data set of like, oh, this is what these things should look like. We actually figured it out for ourselves, and that's an incredible thing that no one has cracked yet in AI. And so to me, that is the essence of what it will take to get to superintelligence, like a system that can just keep learning and discovering knowledge forever.

Speaker 1 | 11:05 - 11:40
So the second element is breadth, that we want something which can do this incredible discovery from all the way to incredible things, and it should be possible to drop it into any stream of experience. So whether it's like a simulated world or a digital world or a physical world, whatever it's dropped into, it should be something it can just learn and learn and learn. So that's the dream. I think if we crack this, then to me, gives rise to a superintelligence that will be like encountering magic. It'll be something which is so profoundly amazing that it will be able to do wonderful things.

Speaker 2 | 11:40 - 11:46
What will it feel like when we first encounter it? Or is it one of these things where you can't predict ahead of time?

Speaker 1 | 11:47 - 12:09
I think it will be amazing. I think we'll we will... You know, that we should have an experience of, like, wonderment. And the only thing I can say from my own experience is what happened when we got to this point in admittedly much narrower field. But when we got there in in in board games, you know, when we got to the point of superhuman play in the game of Go, like, it brought wonderment to the field.

Speaker 1 | 12:09 - 12:37
Like, the Go players who saw, like, AlphaGo playing, you know, they were amazed. Like, it was like a joyful experience for them to kind of witness this kind of Go playing. Same happened when we got to superhuman play in chess, and, you know, the chess players, they they they were so excited. And just imagine, like, going far beyond that, but, like, in, you know, things which are discovering incredible things, new fields of science, new types of technology that we've never even dreamed of. I mean, it will be incredible.

Speaker 2 | 12:37 - 12:57
So the current paradigm, these large language models with reinforcement learning seem to be at least knocking out millennium problems and making some sorts of scientific discoveries. Does that too count as a super learner? Or what's the difference between something that can make novel scientific discoveries versus a super learner in your sense of the term?

Speaker 1 | 12:57 - 13:20
Yeah. So look, I think LLMs are doing a lot of great things, and I have a lot of respect for what's being achieved. What I mean by a super learner is something which, first of all, discovers completely autonomously. And I think what we've seen so far, at least with these kind of approaches that have been taken, is there's a lot of human in the loop effort that's required to make these breakthroughs. It's not fully autonomous yet.

Speaker 1 | 13:20 - 13:59
And it's also something which should be applicable to real world embodied domains where the agent can learn from its physical experience. And we're a long, long, long way off that one. It's not at all clear that LLMs and language based approaches are even the right vehicle to achieve that kind of knowledge. Thinking about these things in terms of language might not even be the right paradigm, and it might just be that all of this human data that's being used in LLMs is kind of weighing things down. So a lot of respect for some of the progress that's made, but I don't think we're anywhere close to this true super learner of something which can be autonomously just discover everything for itself.

Speaker 2 | 13:59 - 14:27
What does building this look like in practice for you? And we backed Janis, who was on your original AlphaGo team, and he told us that one of the things that's distinct about you is you can have these incredibly ambitious visions, but you also ground the team in very practical research milestones. I'd love to understand, big, big, big vision. What does this look like in the day to day and what are you implementing? How do you spend your days right now?

Speaker 1 | 14:27 - 15:13
Yeah, great question. So day to day, I suppose there's a lot of hard technical work by people like Rasa to build the whole stack. That means we've got a state of the art reinforcement learning stack that allows us to run things at massive scale, inhale data at optimal way, be able to kind of learn and have systems that keep learning and learning and learning. And then on top of that, so we've spoken about the super learner. The other aspect which we're building is we're building out environments which are capable of super learners like discovering everything, simulated environments in which a super learner can discover everything that we mean by intelligence.

Speaker 1 | 15:13 - 15:54
We call those crucibles. So they're environments in which it's possible for agents to make incredible discoveries in which it's possible to express and learn everything that we think of as intelligence. And so we have been putting a certain amount of effort into creating these environments. And so it's a combination of building out the super learner, doing the research to make super learners incredible and beat the state of the art of what's possible with reinforcement learning, both in terms of the engineering and the research that happens, and creating and placing the super learners into these crucibles to see the emergence of incredible behaviors. And in terms of the grounding, you asked about how to ground this in the day to day.

Speaker 1 | 15:54 - 16:13
So we ground it in milestones, and the milestones are kind of analogous to what happens with the human journey where we discovered incredible things. And so those become natural milestones for us, for our agents to rediscover the great moments that humans went through in our discovery of knowledge.

Speaker 2 | 16:13 - 16:22
What do you think the agents will rediscover first when that's going to be your first moment of, Oh, this is working?

Speaker 1 | 16:22 - 16:53
I imagine we're going be surprised. Like, I think one thing which is different about the way we take to doing reinforcement learning to a lot of the rest of the field is that we are not breadcrumbs trailing the particular objective to be learnt about. A lot of the way things people do RL with LLMs at the moment is to kind of say, oh, you know, the the agent should be learning about this problem and then this problem and this problem. And after kind of following that trail, we're kind of pulling the agent by its nose towards a particular desired outcome. We're not taking that approach.

Speaker 1 | 16:53 - 17:17
We're giving the agent some simple objectives and asking it to, you know, discover things that will surprise us and amaze us. So, you know, the agent is in principle capable of discovering all kinds of things, and we don't necessarily know in advance what those discoveries will be. And it's kind of just going to be exciting to witness that journey. So I hope to be surprised, I think is the answer to your question.

Speaker 2 | 17:17 - 17:42
Interesting. So what you're saying is instead of explicitly giving the agent the goal to go rediscover language or build a calculator or build a computer, you're going give it other more open ended goals. And the agent may discover that the most efficient way to actually or the best way to actually accomplish that goal may be to build some of these tools that we as humans have already built. Is that one way of putting it?

Speaker 1 | 17:42 - 18:13
That's one way of putting it. I think another way to say it is people often think in RL, oh my god, how do I come up with a a reward function that kind of perfectly specifies this really complicated thing that I want to discover? Like, you know, how can I how can I specify exactly what I mean by science? Or how can I specify exactly what I mean by interesting maths? But there's an alternative, and the alternative is that to give the agent something, you know, really straightforward to optimize, but in a really complex environment where there's a lot to learn about.

Speaker 1 | 18:13 - 19:15
And so it turns out that if you look at the way the world has worked in nature, the pursuit and optimization of very simply easy to describe quantities can often give rise to incredibly hard to describe complexity and emergence. So examples of that would be evolution, which kind of just optimize a kind of survival of the fittest some kind of fitness signal, and the pursuit of fitness gave rise to all of the complexity that we see in life. In the human journey, the pursuit of relatively simple kind of goals that we as humans have gave rise to all of the complex behaviors that humans ultimately acquired and all of the knowledge that we eventually ended up with. So the kind of emergent complexity is much greater than the kind of starting point that it was given. So it wasn't like evolution said, look, hey, humans, here's this idea of science, and you need to get to the most complex science that's out there.

Speaker 1 | 19:16 - 19:53
